developer_request: Change a shared API response field/type used by existing frontend consumers, keep unrelated behavior intact, and prove the current application still works on the new contract.
known_facts: A material API field/type/envelope change can leave downstream frontend types or usages on the previous contract even when the contract document itself is correct.
Acceptance or review evidence produced before the shared contract changes may no longer prove the affected consumers.
The correct repair surface is the set of real current consumers and affected tests/evidence, not every project file.
expected_first_moves: Establish the current contract and implementation baseline before mutation.
Search the current repository for consumers of the changed field/type/interface and identify affected tests, types, runtime flows, and review evidence.
Implement the smallest coherent contract and consumer updates, then re-establish acceptance/regression evidence on the new baseline only for affected slices.
must_preserve: Unrelated consumers and behavior that current evidence shows do not depend on the changed contract.
Current project-native validation and deployment conventions unless the requested behavior requires changing them.
must_not: Treat a successfully edited contract document as proof that its consumers are aligned.
Reuse stale acceptance/review evidence from the old contract for affected consumers.
Restart or rewrite unrelated work merely because one shared contract changed.
lessons: Shared-contract changes are evidence invalidation events, not isolated document edits.
Impact must be discovered from current consumers, then only affected slices are reopened and reverified.
Independent verification is most valuable when it compares current implementation evidence to the governing contract rather than trusting the implementer's completion narrative.
